subtopic: Meanings of Six Sigma
stem: A process is described as performing at a six sigma level. What does this tell you?
options: It has six process steps between input and output
Its customer limits sit six standard deviations from the process average, about 3.4 defects per million opportunities
It has passed six DMAIC tollgate reviews
Six people have been trained as belts on the project
explanation: Sigma is the symbol for standard deviation. A six sigma process has six standard deviations between its average and the nearest customer limit, which corresponds to about 3.4 defects per million opportunities. It describes performance, not structure (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The number six refers to standard deviations, not process steps.
DMAIC has five phases and five tollgates, not six.
Belt counts have nothing to do with sigma level.

subtopic: The Problem Solving Strategy Y = f(x)
stem: In the expression Y = f(x), what does Y represent?
options: The root cause the team must remove
The output or result the project is trying to improve
The number of factors in the process
The financial benefit of the project
explanation: Y is the output measure, the result you care about, such as late deliveries per month. The x's are the inputs and process factors that cause it. The strategy is to improve Y by finding and changing the right x's (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Causes are the x's, not Y.
Y is a single result measure, not a count of factors.
Financial benefit may follow from improving Y but is not what Y stands for.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: A team has just completed a data collection plan, checked that its measurement system is reliable and established the current defect rate. Which DMAIC phase has it finished?
options: Define
Measure
Analyse
Improve
explanation: Data collection plan, verified measurement system and baseline performance are the deliverables of Measure. Define produces the charter; Analyse produces confirmed causes; Improve produces a piloted solution (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Define ends with a charter and customer requirements, before data is collected.
Analyse tests causes; it starts once a baseline exists.
Improve trials solutions, well after the baseline is set.

subtopic: Six Sigma Roles & Responsibilities
stem: Which role selects the project, removes organisational obstacles and approves each tollgate, but does not perform the analysis?
options: Green Belt
Black Belt
Champion
Master Black Belt
explanation: The Champion, also called the sponsor, is the senior manager who owns the business problem. They choose the project, clear obstacles and sign off tollgates. Analysis is done by the Green or Black Belt leading the project (Day 1).
distractor_notes: A Green Belt leads smaller projects and does the analysis part-time.
A Black Belt leads complex projects full-time and does the analysis.
A Master Black Belt coaches belts and runs the programme; they are not the project's sponsor.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: A project team is deciding how to define a "defective invoice". Which source should the definition come from?
options: The voice of the business, because invoices affect cash flow
The voice of the customer, because a defect is a failure to meet a customer requirement
The voice of the employee, because staff know which invoices are hard to produce
The Black Belt's judgement, because they have the most training
explanation: A defect is any output that fails a customer requirement, so the definition of a defective invoice must come from what the customer needs. The business and employee voices matter for why the project is funded and where causes lie, but not for defining defects (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The voice of the business explains why the project matters, not what counts as a defect.
The voice of the employee helps find causes, not define requirements.
Requirements come from customers, not from the belt's opinion.

subtopic: General History of Six Sigma & Continuous Improvement
stem: Where did Six Sigma originate?
options: Toyota, Japan, in the 1950s
Motorola, United States, in the 1980s
General Electric, United States, in the 1990s
Ford, United States, in the 1910s
explanation: Six Sigma was developed at Motorola in the 1980s, with engineer Bill Smith usually credited. General Electric adopted and popularised it in the 1990s. Toyota is the origin of Lean, not Six Sigma (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Toyota is where Lean came from.
GE made Six Sigma famous but did not invent it.
Ford's assembly line influenced Lean thinking but is not the origin of Six Sigma.

subtopic: General History of Six Sigma & Continuous Improvement
stem: Lean thinking developed mainly from which source?
options: The Toyota Production System
Motorola's quality programme
The United States military's sampling standards
Bell Laboratories' control chart work
explanation: Lean grew out of the Toyota Production System, developed in Japan after the Second World War by engineers including Taiichi Ohno. It focuses on removing waste so value flows faster (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Motorola is the origin of Six Sigma.
Military sampling standards contributed to acceptance sampling, not Lean.
Bell Labs (Walter Shewhart) gave us control charts, which are a Six Sigma tool.

subtopic: Meanings of Six Sigma
stem: Which statement best distinguishes the focus of Lean from the focus of Six Sigma?
options: Lean reduces variation; Six Sigma removes waste
Lean removes waste and delay; Six Sigma reduces variation and defects
Lean applies to manufacturing; Six Sigma applies to services
Lean uses statistics; Six Sigma uses visual management
explanation: Lean asks which steps add value and removes the rest, attacking waste and delay. Six Sigma asks how much output varies from requirements and finds the causes of that variation. Both apply to any industry (Day 1).
distractor_notes: This reverses the two.
Both methods apply to manufacturing and services alike.
Statistics belong mainly to Six Sigma; visual management is a Lean tool.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: Which deliverable belongs to the Control phase?
options: Project charter
Baseline defect rate
Control plan and monitoring chart handed to the process owner
List of confirmed root causes
explanation: Control makes sure the improvement lasts: a control plan, monitoring charts and updated procedures are handed to the process owner. The charter is Define, the baseline is Measure and confirmed causes are Analyse (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The charter is produced in Define.
The baseline is produced in Measure.
Confirmed causes are the output of Analyse.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: What is the purpose of a tollgate review?
options: To let the team choose which DMAIC phase to do next
To have the sponsor confirm a phase's deliverables are complete before the next phase starts
To measure the process capability at the end of the project
To train Yellow Belts in the tools used so far
explanation: A tollgate is the review at the end of each phase where the Champion checks the deliverables and approves moving on. DMAIC phases run in a fixed order, so the review is about readiness, not choosing a direction (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The phase order is fixed: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control.
Capability is measured in Measure and rechecked in Control, not at tollgates as such.
Training is not the purpose of a tollgate.

subtopic: The Problem Solving Strategy Y = f(x)
stem: A call centre wants to cut average call handling time. A team member proposes "measure handling time every day and display it on a big screen so people try harder." In terms of Y = f(x), what is the weakness of this proposal?
options: It measures the wrong Y; call volume should be measured instead
It acts only on Y and does not identify or change any x that causes long calls
It uses too many x's at once
It confuses the voice of the customer with the voice of the business
explanation: Handling time is the Y. Displaying Y more prominently does not change the causes of long calls, such as system lookups, unclear scripts or call transfers. Y = f(x) says you change results by changing the x's that drive them (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Handling time is a reasonable Y for this problem.
The proposal names no x's at all.
The proposal is not about which voice is used.

subtopic: Six Sigma Roles & Responsibilities
stem: Which description best fits a Green Belt?
options: Works full-time on improvement and leads complex cross-functional projects
Leads smaller projects in their own area, usually part-time alongside a normal job
Trains Black Belts and manages the organisation's improvement programme
Owns the business problem and funds the project
explanation: Green Belts keep their normal role and lead smaller, local projects part-time. Black Belts are full-time on complex projects, Master Black Belts coach and run the programme, and the Champion owns and funds the problem (Day 1).
distractor_notes: That describes a Black Belt.
That describes a Master Black Belt.
That describes the Champion or sponsor.

subtopic: Six Sigma Roles & Responsibilities
stem: At the end of the Control phase, who takes responsibility for keeping the improved process running day to day?
options: The Master Black Belt
The Green Belt who led the project
The process owner
The Champion
explanation: The process owner is the manager responsible for the process in normal operation. Control ends with handover to them, including the control plan and monitoring charts. The belt moves on to the next project (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The Master Black Belt coaches belts; they do not run processes.
The Green Belt hands the process back and moves to other work.
The Champion sponsors projects; the process owner runs the process.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: "Each late shipment costs us about $9 in refunds, which is roughly $13 000 a month." Which voice is this statement an example of?
options: Voice of the customer
Voice of the business
Voice of the employee
Voice of the process
explanation: Cost, margin and financial impact are the voice of the business: they explain why the organisation should fund the project. The customer's voice would describe what "late" means to them; the employee's voice would describe obstacles in doing the work (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Customers care about receiving parcels on time, not about the company's refund costs.
Employees' voice is about how the work feels and where it goes wrong.
"Voice of the process" describes measured process behaviour, not money.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: Which of these is the most direct method of collecting the voice of the customer?
options: Reviewing the annual budget
Interviewing customers and analysing their complaints
Reading the team's shift handover notes
Calculating the process sigma level
explanation: The voice of the customer is gathered from customers themselves: interviews, surveys, complaints and observation. Budgets are the voice of the business, handover notes the voice of the employee, and sigma level is a process measure (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The budget reflects the business's needs, not the customer's.
Handover notes capture the employee's view.
Sigma level is a measurement of the process, not a customer input.

subtopic: Meanings of Six Sigma
stem: Which statement about the term "sigma" is correct?
options: Sigma is the Greek letter used for the mean of a population
Sigma is the Greek letter used for standard deviation, a measure of spread
Sigma is the number of defects found per unit
Sigma is the number of steps in a process
explanation: Sigma (σ) is the statistical symbol for standard deviation, which measures how spread out values are. The mean is written μ (mu). Defects per unit and step counts have their own names (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The population mean is μ, not σ.
Defects per unit is DPU.
Step count is not a statistical symbol.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: A team ran a two-week trial of a new sorting screen on one shift and showed the late-parcel rate fell from 12% to 7% on that shift. Which phase does this work belong to, and what should come next?
options: Analyse; next, write the project charter
Improve; next, build a control plan and hand over to the process owner
Measure; next, brainstorm causes
Control; next, pilot the solution on other shifts
explanation: Piloting a solution and showing it moves Y is the Improve phase. The next phase is Control: standardise the change, set up monitoring and hand over so the gain holds. Charters come first (Define) and cause-finding is Analyse (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Analyse finds causes; the charter was written back in Define.
Measure establishes the baseline before causes are tested.
Piloting belongs to Improve; Control comes after the pilot succeeds.

subtopic: General History of Six Sigma & Continuous Improvement
stem: Why were Lean and Six Sigma combined into a single method?
options: Because Six Sigma had been discredited and needed a new name
Because a process can be fast but error-prone, or accurate but slow, and the two methods address these different problems
Because Lean only works in Japan and Six Sigma only works in the United States
Because regulators required both
explanation: Lean attacks delay and waste; Six Sigma attacks variation and defects. A process usually needs both. Combining them lets one project use whichever tools the problem calls for (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Six Sigma was not discredited; it remains widely used.
Both methods are used worldwide across industries.
No regulator requires either method.

subtopic: The Problem Solving Strategy Y = f(x)
stem: In Y = f(x), which of the following is an example of an x rather than a Y?
options: Percentage of orders shipped late
Number of complaints per month
Which supplier provided the packaging
Average minutes to resolve a ticket
explanation: The supplier used is an input factor that may cause a result, so it is an x. The other three are all output measures (results) and would be Y's (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Late shipment percentage is a result, so it is a Y.
Complaints per month is a result: a Y.
Resolution time is a result: a Y.

subtopic: Six Sigma Roles & Responsibilities
stem: Which role provides basic awareness-level support, such as helping to collect data during a project?
options: Yellow Belt
Black Belt
Champion
Master Black Belt
explanation: Yellow Belts (and White Belts in some schemes) have basic training and support projects as team members, often collecting data or joining improvement events. The other roles lead, coach or sponsor (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Black Belts lead complex projects full-time.
The Champion sponsors the project.
The Master Black Belt coaches belts and runs the programme.
